question.text: Deepak withdrew his EPF balance of Rs.8,50,000 after working for 4 years and 10 months in his company. He then joined a new firm. What is the tax treatment of this EPF withdrawal?

answer.text: Fully exempt as EPF withdrawals are always tax-free
Fully taxable as continuous service is less than 5 years
Exempt up to Rs.5,00,000 and balance taxable
Taxable only on the interest component, principal is exempt

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook states that an EPF withdrawal before completing five consecutive years of service is taxable in the year of receipt, unless a listed exception applies or the balance is transferred to the new employer's PF account. Deepak's service was 4 years and 10 months — short of the five-year threshold — and he chose to withdraw rather than transfer, so the workbook treats the entire withdrawal as taxable. The Trap: Option A repeats the common misconception that EPF is always tax-free; the EEE status is conditional on completing five years (or qualifying for an exception or transferring to the new employer). Option C invents a Rs.5,00,000 exemption threshold — the Rs.50,000 figure that appears in the EPF discussion is a TDS/tax-payment threshold, not an exemption ceiling. Option D invents a principal-versus-interest split. Note: The clean rule from the workbook: a withdrawal before five years is taxable unless an exception applies, while a transfer of the PF balance to the new employer preserves the continuous-service clock and the tax-favoured status.
